item.title: Our Social Brains Couldn't Hang Up on the Telephone
item.description:
Creativity

Our Social Brains Couldn't Hang Up on the Telephone

The invention from 1876 transformed social communication as we knew it.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • The invention of the telephone offered a way to communicate without seeing other people.
  • That transformation may have perplexed our socially driven brains.
  • Our brains don't get software updates, leaving them to adapt to new technology.
Bell's invention allowed people to talk without seeing each other.
Source: Momentmal/Pixabay

The telephone turned 150 years old this year. The request of the first ever call, from Alexander Graham Bell to Thomas A. Watson, was simple. “Mr. Watson, come here. I want to see you.”

Bell was a professor of vocal physiology at Boston University at that time, and his patent for this new device was entitled, “Improvement on Telegraphy.”

He likely didn’t ponder his influence on social health. For the first time in human history, people could communicate in real time without seeing each other.

While people must have marveled at the transformative way to converse, the human brain was probably perplexed. Totally absent were non-verbal cues, body language, and pheromones in communicating with one another.

After all, human brains were accustomed to a face-to-face social world for eons. People lived together in communities, worked in groups, and explored in teams.

However, the phone, and other subsequent technology, ushered in a period where transactions can be absent of human interaction. People can now live more independently than ever before, yet, as psychologist Nicholas Epley wrote in his book A Little More Social, “Your Stone Age brain wasn’t built for this.”

In some ways, the brain and communication technology don’t really mesh. In his book Why Brains Need Friends, neuroscientist Ben Rein pointed out that phones and computers get regular software updates. Unfortunately, our brains don’t.

The upside is that it isn’t an adapt-or-perish situation. “The people who can’t figure out an iPhone won’t die because of it,” Rein told me via email. “There’s no evolutionary pressure for our brains to get any better at using technology.”

In his book, he likened the three-pound organ inside our skulls to “a horse-drawn carriage on the autobahn” when it comes to the virtual world.

That slow-paced social brain isn’t going to change in an internet world of conversing. On top of that, “The autobahn is only going to get faster and faster,” he said.

Researchers Faraji and Metz (2023) acknowledged that “many open questions and challenges for uncovering the social brain’s complexities remain to be addressed.”

Our socially driven brains may favor Bell’s line when it comes to communicating with others. Instead of a text or an email, it may be requesting, “I want to see you.”

article continues after advertisement

Those face-to-face times, though, may be dwindling.

item.title: Financial Infidelity or Financial Abuse?
item.description:
Infidelity

Financial Infidelity or Financial Abuse?

Knowing the difference between harmful financial behaviors can change everything.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Financial issues are at the heart of many marital problems I see in my legal practice.
  • Financial infidelity occurs when one partner intentionally conceals financial information from the other.
  • In financial abuse, the primary goal is control and gaining, and keeping, power.
  • Whether the issue is financial infidelity or financial abuse, ignoring it rarely makes it disappear.
Source: Mikhail Nilov/Pexels

As is well known, money is one of the leading sources of conflict in couples, and it is true in my practice as a family law attorney.

The issues can range from what the family chooses to spend money on, to how much they are saving, to more granular issues like whether they should send their children to private school or how to pay for college and retirement.

But these are fairly typical discussions, and those I would encourage every couple to talk about openly, honestly, and often. But not every financial discussion is the same.

There are two terms that come up in my practice that are presumed to be interchangeable but actually are not: “financial infidelity” and “financial abuse.”

Knowing the difference is important. One primarily involves secrecy, which can lead to broken trust, while the other involves an attempt to gain power and control.

As a divorce attorney, I have seen both. Sometimes a spouse hides a credit card, secretly accumulates debt, or makes secret purchases. The motive in these cases might be embarrassment or fear of conflict. That’s what I would characterize as “financial infidelity.”

But in other cases, a partner controls every dollar the spouse can access, which can leave them financially dependent and lead to a host of other problems. This is one form of “financial abuse.”

Both situations can certainly break trust and damage a marriage, but they require very different responses. Here are a few of the signs and repercussions of each:

Financial Infidelity

  • One partner intentionally conceals financial information from the other. This may include opening a secret bank account, building up and then hiding credit card debt, or making large purchases without disclosure.
  • They may gamble, lend money to family members, or have an undisclosed form of income, each without the other spouse knowing.
  • Financial infidelity breaks trust. It undermines transparency and can leave the other spouse questioning what else has been hidden.
  • Financial infidelity does not necessarily involve an effort to dominate or control the relationship. A spouse may hide spending for a host of reasons, including shame about debt or anxiety over disappointing their partner. This does not excuse the behavior, but it does distinguish it from abuse.

Financial Abuse

In financial abuse, the primary goal is control. It is a form of emotional abuse.

A financially abusive partner uses money and access to money to create dependence and limit the other person's freedom. A financially abusive partner may, among other things:

  • Restrict access to the couple’s financial information.
  • Refuse to share passwords to joint accounts, including bank accounts, credit cards, mortgages, or car payments.
  • Monitor the purchases their partner makes.
  • Prevent the partner from working, including sabotaging career opportunities.
  • One spouse may insist the other lives on an “allowance” while they spend money however they would like.

The objective is not to keep a secret. It is to weaken the other spouse and maintain power.

In many abusive relationships, the victimized spouse has little or no knowledge of the family's financial picture and no way to access that information. This can lead to a feeling of despair, as leaving a relationship can feel impossible without access to financial resources.

Of course, financial infidelity and financial abuse can occur together. A controlling spouse may also hide assets or secretly move money to maintain leverage. Further, repeated financial deception can evolve into financial abuse if it is used to manipulate or intimidate the other partner.

One of the ways this manifests in my practice is that people can normalize unhealthy financial dynamics by telling themselves, "My spouse has always managed the financial side of things" or "I'm just not good with money.”

To be clear, in many healthy marriages, one spouse manages “the books” while the other oversees other aspects of the busy family and children. The key difference between a healthy relationship and an unhealthy one is transparency. So, if one spouse wants to understand the finances, the one who is overseeing the finances should be open and honest and answer all of their partner’s questions.

If you are wondering if you or a loved one is a victim of financial infidelity or financial abuse, here are a few questions to ask yourself:

  • Do you know where your family's assets are held and how to access that information?
  • Can you access money without going through your spouse if you need it?
  • Do you make major financial decisions as a couple?
  • Do you feel comfortable asking questions about money and gaining access to financial information without fear of criticism or retaliation?

If you answer “no” to any of the above, you probably should take time to have a conversation with your partner, and if he or she is not interested in discussing the topic, it may be time to take a closer look at the financial dynamics in your relationship.

Whether the issue is financial infidelity or financial abuse, ignoring it does nothing. The good news is that some financial conflicts can be repaired—I have seen it happen. Honest communication, transparency, and professional guidance can help many couples rebuild trust after financial infidelity.

Addressing financial abuse, however, will likely require more work. When money is used to isolate, intimidate, or manipulate, you will need to try to find the root of these control issues and achieve an understanding from the abuser’s perspective that access to financial information is not optional. It is required for a healthy relationship.

If you identify with any of this, as I always say, please take care of yourself and your family during what can be a very stressful time.
